Insular isolation: A more obvious form of isolation are those species or subspecies that are endemic to an island or group of islands. Most notable are 31 native Hawaiian forms of birds and mammals most of which are threatened with extinction. Not only are these species and subspecies vulnerable because their available habitat is limited to one or a few islands, but their particular niche or association on those islands may be, and usually is, disappearing. Of the 31 Hawaiian species and subspecies, 22 are endemic to just one island. Seven species and subspecies in Puerto Rico are threatened. As in Hawaii, survival of each is threatened by disappearance of the ecological association to which the animal is endemic. Other species and subspecies listed in the "Red Book" are isolated on islands more closely associated with the continent. Successful restoration of any of these insular species or subspecies would, of course, affect the physical environment of only the island or islands to which they were endemic.
<u>Economic environment</u>: The economic environment or climate is the existing potential for generating or affecting economic return. The existing endangered species program already demonstrates that listing, management and restoration of endangered species can affect the economic environment.
It would be highly rewarding to develope a format for quantifying the economic impact of this legislation, or even for the operation of an endangered species program in general. At this time no such capability is available. Strict cash flow analysis falls far short of adequacy in this regard. While it is perhaps possible to quantify the direct expenditures in program funds earmarked specifically for endangered species, there is not yet any acceptable method for estimating long term indirect costs of these programs.
